solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: See 19
Personal target? Not for 19/1

parts.note: something personal is your own
a goal is a target to aim at

explanation.surface: A private aim, but one a famous striker would rather avoid.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: a goal put into your own net is the last thing the Portuguese striker wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward lives to score at the other end; putting the ball into his own team's net is the opposite of his job.

clue.text: Non-U relative runs away with lover — they're found in Africa

indicators.note: Non-U says the letter U is to be taken away from the next word

parts.note: an aunt is a family relative
to elope is to run off secretly with a lover

explanation.surface: A not-quite-posh relative runs off with a sweetheart, and the pair turn up in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-U' is also British slang for socially unrefined, which is the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Many species of these swift horned grazing animals live on the African savannah.

clue.text: Resting place variously occupied by dead

indicators.note: variously occupied suggests the letters are filled into different positions, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A grave or tomb filled with assorted dead bodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resting place' suggests a cemetery, but it is a couch; 'variously occupied' rearranges BY DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A couch used for lying down by day is literally a place for resting.

clue.text: The Leaky Cauldron? It's found in Hertfordshire

definitions.meaning: the Leaky Cauldron is the pub in the Harry Potter books, so it is the young wizard's drinking place
a town in the county of Hertfordshire, just north of London

explanation.surface: A fictional wizards' pub is placed in an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hertfordshire commuter town's name also reads as the pub belonging to the boy wizard; Hertfordshire is a county north of London.

clue.text: Not even the Shadow Chancellor is nuts

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd
Ed Balls was Labour's Shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer at the time

explanation.surface: A jibe that the opposition's finance spokesman is crazy, and not even slightly.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts as a noun means eccentric or crazy people, the same as weirdos.

clue.text: Count for one and let it out

indicators.note: out suggests the words have been put out of order, rearranged

explanation.surface: Tally up for a single person and release it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a verb but is the nobleman, an example of the defined word, as 'for one' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Count is a rank of nobility, so it is one example of an honorific such as Duke or Lord.

clue.text: 1's first three dribbles initially impress adult in 9 — it's poetry!

indicators.note: first three says keep only the opening trio of letters of the footballer's surname and drop the rest

parts.note: 1-across is the footballer's surname

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of the next word
in says the adult goes inside the union from 9-down

parts.note: 9-down is the European Union, abbreviated EU
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: The star dribbles and impresses grown-ups in Europe, and his play is poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impress' and 'in' together say A is pressed into EU; 9 refers to EUROPEAN UNION, shortened to its usual abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A short French verse form with a refrain, so it is a kind of poetry.

clue.text: International arrangement in marriage of Victoria and Albert?

definitions.meaning: a bloc of member states bound by treaty
Victoria was British and Albert German, so their wedding joined two people from the continent

explanation.surface: Asking whether the famous royal wedding was a kind of treaty between nations.
explanation.definitionFit: The political bloc of states is an international arrangement, and a wedding of two continentals is a union of Europeans.

clue.text: It's not typical to have this kind of nose

indicators.note: to have says the opening words contain the letters, held within them

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain sort of nose is unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'It's not typical'.
explanation.definitionFit: A runny nose full of mucus is described with this informal adjective.

clue.text: Getting newer version or punching above your weight?

definitions.meaning: bringing something up to the latest edition
going out with someone more attractive than yourself, read as dating up

explanation.surface: Upgrading something, or aiming higher than you should.
explanation.definitionFit: Refreshing software is the usual sense; read as up-dating it means courting someone out of your league.

clue.text: See 5
Audience's encouragement to Westwood who's in a handy sporting position?

definitions.text: who's in a handy sporting position

indicators.note: an audience hears things, so this is what the words sound like

parts.note: Lee Westwood is an English golfer, so a fan would cheer go, Lee

explanation.surface: Golf fans shout support to a player who is in a good position.
explanation.walkthrough: The keeper is the only footballer allowed to use hands, hence 'handy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The keeper is the one player who may handle the ball, a position that is literally handy.

clue.text: Working to get qualification in the same class

parts.note: a machine that is working is on
the A level is the British school-leaving exam taken at 18

explanation.surface: Studying for an exam alongside classmates.
explanation.walkthrough: A levels are the exams English pupils take at 18.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things at the same level are equal, matched in standing or rank.

clue.text: Knocked back continental beer in a smooth movement

indicators.note: knocked back suggests the word is sent backwards, reading from the end

parts.note: Pils is a pale lager in the Pilsner style from continental Europe

explanation.surface: Downing a foreign lager in one easy swig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' looks like drinking but turns PILS around.
explanation.definitionFit: A slide or glide is an easy sliding motion.

clue.text: Young Blair, individual leaving Oxford University, formed this?

definitions.text: Young Blair, individual leaving Oxford University, formed this?

parts.note: something young is new

indicators.note: formed says the letters are moulded into another shape
leaving says one piece goes away from the name

parts.note: the former Prime Minister's surname
I, the Roman numeral one, stands for an individual

explanation.surface: The young Tony Blair, fresh from Oxford, created the rebranded party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' takes I from BLAIR, giving BLAR; 'formed' rearranges BLAR with OU. Tony Blair, an Oxford graduate, built the 1990s rebrand of his party.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1990s rebrand of the Labour Party was the creation of Tony Blair.

clue.text: Indication of departure as result of Mandelson's defecting?

definitions.meaning: a flag hoisted when a ship is about to sail
Peter Mandelson was a Labour grandee; if he crossed to the Conservatives, whose colour is blue, he would become a Tory Peter

explanation.surface: A Labour figure switching sides might signal he is leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The blue and white naval flag signals a vessel is ready to sail; Conservatives are the blue party in Britain.

clue.text: Thoroughly punctures slicks? They're shafted!

indicators.note: punctures says one piece pierces into the middle of another

parts.note: oil slicks are spills of oil
doing something well means doing it thoroughly

explanation.surface: Something that pierces oil spills, and the victims are stitched up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shafted' looks like slang for cheated but means fitted with a shaft.
explanation.definitionFit: These drilled boreholes are literally shafts sunk into the ground.

clue.text: Footballer's social nadir — or not possibly?

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters of the following words could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A question about a famous player's worst moment in society, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SOCIAL NADIR OR NOT, rearranged as 'possibly' allows, give the Portuguese star's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Portuguese forward is one of the most famous players in world football.

clue.text: Half-cut Bogart's motley crew?

indicators.note: motley means jumbled and multicoloured, so the letters are mixed up
half-cut says cut the name in half and keep the latter part

parts.note: a pack is a gang or crew

explanation.surface: A drunken film star's ragtag band of friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' looks like British slang for tipsy but keeps the back half of the name, ART, which 'motley' scrambles.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of the boozy Hollywood social circle around Bogart, later led by Sinatra.

clue.text: Admitting Greece into 9 viewed, in retrospect, as impulse

indicators.note: in retrospect means looking back, so the result is read from end to start
admitting says one piece is let into another

parts.note: 9-down is the European Union, abbreviated EU
GR is the international abbreviation for Greece

explanation.surface: Letting Greece into the European Union looks, with hindsight, like a rash decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 is EUROPEAN UNION, used in its short form; 'in retrospect' turns EGRU around.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden strong desire to act is a compulsion or drive.

clue.text: Artist's judging unfinished university installation

indicators.note: installation says one piece is fitted inside another
unfinished says the last letter is cut off

parts.note: gauging something means judging or estimating it

explanation.surface: A critic assessing an incomplete art installation at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts GAUGING to GAUGIN, and 'installation' fits U inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Gauguin was the French Post-Impressionist painter famous for his Tahiti canvases.

clue.text: Claimants receive couple of royalties in bum case

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other
case says the outer word wraps around like a casing

parts.note: ass is slang for the backside
K for king and ER for Elizabeth Regina, the queen, make a royal pair

explanation.surface: Plaintiffs collect royalty payments in a hopeless lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum case' sounds like a worthless lawsuit; ER is the Queen's royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: People who make claims or requests are those who ask for something.

clue.text: Sweating, knackered, but just the result Cavendish wanted

indicators.note: knackered, British slang for worn out or broken, says the letters are damaged into a new order

explanation.surface: A cyclist drenched and exhausted, yet victorious.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Cavendish is a British sprint cyclist famed for winning Tour de France legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning a single leg of a cycling tour was the sprinter's main goal in each race.

clue.text: Paris Match perhaps about to include its article exposing Sheen

indicators.note: to include says one piece is taken inside the other
about says the word turns round

parts.note: Paris Match is a French magazine, a mag
Paris Match is French, so its definite article is le

explanation.surface: A French magazine is about to run a story revealing an actor named Sheen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns MAG into GAM. Since Paris Match is French, 'its article' is French too. 'Sheen' looks like the actor Martin or Charlie Sheen.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheen is a soft shine or glow on a surface.

clue.text: After a month, hesitation that becomes deviated possibly

indicators.note: after says the hesitation is placed following the month

parts.note: Sept is the short form of September
um is the sound of a pause in speech

explanation.surface: After a month of dithering, something goes astray.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'deviated septum' is a common nasal condition, so the definition names the part that can become deviated.
explanation.definitionFit: The wall between the nostrils can be bent off-centre, a condition doctors describe as deviated.

clue.text: Mein Kampf penned in this?

indicators.note: penned means enclosed, as in a pen, so the letters are held inside the title

explanation.surface: Was Hitler's book written with a pen and this?
explanation.walkthrough: 'penned' looks like 'written' but signals the letters held inside 'Mein Kampf'.
explanation.definitionFit: A book is written with pen and this fluid, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Heated clash in Europe about ordering of eau de toilette?

parts.note: eau is French for water
toilette suggests toilet, for which loo is British slang

explanation.surface: A fierce fight over the arrangement of a perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: Translating the French words of 'eau de toilette' in their printed order gives the battle's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1815 battle in Belgium where Wellington defeated Napoleon was a fierce European clash.

clue.text: Go to restaurant for tea, perhaps?

parts.note: the instruction to rearrange the letters of eat produces the word tea

explanation.surface: Dining out to have an afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, the answer says take EAT and mix it up, which gives TEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a meal away from home at a restaurant or café.

clue.text: Face cover-up as crack troops capture Jong-un, leader of Korea

indicators.note: capture says the troops hold the captive inside them

parts.note: the SAS is Britain's elite Special Air Service regiment
Kim Jong-un is the North Korean leader

indicators.note: leader of means the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Special forces in disguise seize North Korea's ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: SAS is Britain's Special Air Service.
explanation.definitionFit: A woollen balaclava hides the face, so it is literally a covering for it.

clue.text: In America, Fanny's seen wearing this?

definitions.text: In America, Fanny's seen wearing this?

parts.words: In America, Fanny's seen wearing this?
parts.note: in American English fanny means the backside, which this skimpy garment leaves on show

explanation.definitionFit: A tiny thong leaves the buttocks visible, so a bottom is seen wearing one.
